utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Unfortunately we'll continue to sit pursuant to 15 bis, with Judge Lattanzi being away due to her flu. There are a couple of matters I would like to deal with before we continue to hear the evidence. The Chamber first refers to the objection raised by Mr. Robinson during the testimony of KW570 on the 18th of January, 2013, regarding the use of leading questions in cross-examination to elicit relevant evidence not raised in direct examination and not going to the credibility of the witness pursuant to Rule 90(H). The Chamber notes that, as submitted by Mr. Robinson, the Prlic Trial Chamber in its decision on Prosecution motion concerning use of leading questions of the 4th of July, 2008, did impose guide-lines in that case which prevented the use of leading questions in relation to cross-examination conducted pursuant to Rule 90(H) on matters not raised in direct examination. This approach is not consistent with that taken by this Chamber in exercising its control over the conduct of this case and the admission of evidence pursuant to Rule 90(H). Indeed, during the Prosecution case, the Chamber adopted an interpretation of Rule 90(H) which allowed the accused to adduce evidence relevant to his case during his cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses and did not preclude him from using leading questions during such cross-examination. The Chamber is of the view that this interpretation is consistent with the plain wording of Rule 90(H), which speaks of cross-examination throughout. In addition, to apply a different standard now would be contrary to the interests of justice. Having said that, this Chamber noted in the pre-Defence conference on the 15th of October, 2012, that "while the Prosecution may make use of Rule 90(H) during the Defence case, it must limit itself to a reasonable exercise of that rule." The Chamber will continue to exercise control over the use of Rule 90(H) and the manner in which cross-examination is conducted, including the use of leading questions to ensure that the rights of the accused are protected and the interests of justice are not compromised. For the next matter, the Chamber will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless there's any other matter. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just to advise you of the latest with respect to our schedule and order of witnesses. The Prosecution indicated to us this morning that they would not be prepared to commence the cross-examination of Colonel Indjic after his direct examination. So after we complete the testimony of the current witness, we'll have the direct examination of Colonel Indjic, followed by the direct examination of Dragomir Milosevic. However, if we were not to have completed the direct examination of General Milosevic by the end of the day on Wednesday, we would ask the Prosecution -- we would ask that his testimony be interrupted so that Colonel Indjic can complete his cross-examination by the end of this week, which would be Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've been in communication with Ms. Edgerton, who will be leading or will be cross-examining the witness. This particular proposal wasn't broached. I think it's probably consistent with the expectations that we had. But before affirming that understanding, I'd like to double-check; but I think that's going to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, when do you expect the evidence of Milosevic to start?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: At approximately 12.00. I estimated around 12.00 today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. We'll bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mijanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mijanovic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yesterday when we concluded I was asking you some questions about the claim at paragraph 6 of your statement, that the authorities of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza did not expel any non-Serbs and that they moved out on their own and in an unorganised manner. And I'd like to continue with some more questions to you about that claim. Gornji Kotorac is a settlement in Ilidza where there were Muslims living before the war; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And is it your position that the Muslims of Gornji Kotorac moved out of their own accord and in an unorganised manner?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I feel like a poor student here. You're asking me all these difficult questions and you look like the headmaster of my old school. Let me explain. The Serb Ilidza, when I came there it was divided physically into two sections that were not linked. Gornji Kotorac remained in that other part that was out of reach for me during the war and I don't think I went even once for the duration; therefore, I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, be comforted. You probably looked more like head mistress.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So even though you've claimed in your statement that the Muslims in Ilidza moved out in an unorganised manner of their own accord, you're saying now that you can't really speak to what happened to some of the Muslims in Ilidza in parts of the municipality that you didn't go to; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Could we go to P1086, please. I'd just like to show you a few documents about the Muslims of Gornji Kotorac, starting with this document which is an intercept between Mr. Prstojevic and a certain Milenko and then Mr. Prstojevic and a certain Novakovic. On page 1 there are introductions, and if we go to page 2 Prstojevic asks a few lines down: "Why did Mika phone me?" And Milenko says: "Phoned you to check with you, these people in Kotorac." Milenko says: "What should we do with them? And Prstojevic says: "Did you arrest them? What did you do?" And then a few lines down Mr. Prstojevic says: "And where are those people? Have they been arrested?" And then Milenko says: "Down there on the road all of them men are separated from women." And Prstojevic says: "Ha." And then Milenko says: "Just a second." And he says then: "I've just received the word, men are in the Kula prison and women went in the direction of Butmir." And Prstojevic says: "Put Tepavcevic on." And Milenko says: "Here's Novakovic." And in the background he says: "It's Prstojevic, stop fooling around." And then Novakovic and Prstojevic have introductions. If we could go to the next page in the B/C/S. Prstojevic asks: "Have you been cleaning Kotorac today" -- sorry, Mr. Mijanovic, is something funny? I'm asking you, Mr. Mijanovic, you're laughing. Is something funnily?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the expressions here I find to be a bit rustic in the text itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So is the expression "have you been cleaning Kotorac today," is that one of the expressions you find rustic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. And Novakovic responds: "They have. I don't know the exact details because I was engaged otherwise." And a few lines down Prstojevic says: "That's okay, but tell me, please, I beg of you, why did you take the women to Butmir?" And Novakovic said: "They said women were not in Butmir -- but, well, in Butmir, yes, not to KP Dom but to Butmir. That's where they're going." Prstojevic says: "They cannot go to Butmir. We'll mop up Butmir in time as well." On the next page he says: "Butmir will be mopped up. Sokolovic will be mopped up. Hrasnica will be mopped up." So Novakovic says: "Well, I don't know where to take them." And Prstojevic says: "There is Bascarsija, please take all of them to Bascarsija on foot." And Novakovic says: "Aha, aha." Prstojevic says: "Women." And: "Men to prison." Novakovic says: "Okay, I'll check with them now and then I'll let you know." And Prstojevic says: "Yes, tell them those who convert to Orthodox religion on the spot they can stay, women and children." And Novakovic says: "Okay." And Prstojevic says: "Do it, please, but don't make mistakes ... you've done an excellent job but it means that Butmir will be mopped up in time. Tell that to the people there." If we could now go to P1126, and this is a letter from the police station at Kula to the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Ministry of Justice, to the attention of the under-secretary and the minister respectively. And the subject is problems regarding persons detained at KP Dom Kula Butmir. And it says that between the 12th of May and the 20th of May there were 156 persons detained at KP Dom Butmir and in the next paragraph it says where they're from, 38 persons were brought in from the TO Ilidza, Kasindolska Street and they were in possession of automatic weapons. And then it says 47 persons from Gornji Kotorac were moved in an operation by former JNA and TO Kasindol forces but returned to the area of Gornji Kotorac on 12 May 1992 and were therefore taken to KP Dom Butmir. And then it refers to other people taken in from Dobrinja, Nedzarici, Vraca, Lukavica, Vojkovici, Ilidza, et cetera. And in the last paragraph on the next page in the English it refers to inadequate conditions of accommodation, food, hygiene, and says it is -- emphasises the urgency in resolving the future status of these detainees. And if we could go to D1243, page 10 in the English and page 19 in the B/C/S. This is a page from the Kula Butmir prison duty transfer log. It's about to appear on your screen. And you see the heading there. It says the list of persons brought from Gornji Kotorac on 12 May 1992, and there is a list of names starting with Rahmo Sehic and then a number of people with the surname Sarajkic. And then if we could go to the next page in the B/C/S. If you could just scan your eyes through that list and confirm that these are all Muslim male names. And if we go to the next page in the English as well, and there are a few more names on the next page in both languages if we could go to the top of the next page. There are in total 47 names listed here, the same number as identified in the letter we just saw, and those are all names of Muslim men, aren't they, Mr. Mijanovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could look at one last document on this topic which is P1151. And this document that you're about to see is another letter from the Kula police station, again to the minister of justice and the under-secretary for the Ministry of the Interior and it refers to our document 592 dated 20 May 1992, which is a document we looked at a few moments ago from the Kula police station. And it says that in our document we informed you of certain issues relating to accommodation, meals, hygiene, et cetera. And in the second paragraph it says: "After co-ordinating with the minister of justice and the SJB undersecretary on 20 May 1992, 114 persons were taken to the Vrbanja bridge location and sent into the city via M. Sokolovic Street. This group consists of persons whose place of residence was in Gornji Kotorac and Dobrinja. "As they were detained since 12 May 1992, and since the Ilidza exchange bureau was informed on two occasions about the possible exchange but did not respond in time, and due to the aforementioned objective problems, it was estimated that this group of detainees should be sent to the aforementioned location." And then it goes on to discuss the problem of the 38 persons from Kasindolska Street who were in possession of weapons and who it was concluded were not -- should not be exchanged. Now, we've seen an intercept from Mr. Prstojevic that was dated the 14th of May, although Mr. Prstojevic's evidence indicated that it should have been, in fact, the 12th of May. And I refer to transcript page 13859. We have two letters from the Kula police station referring to the detention of the Muslim men from Gornji Kotorac after Prstojevic had instructed that they be indeed detained at Kula and the women and children sent to Bascarsija unless they converted to Orthodox on the spot. And the Kula police station letter confirming that the men from Gornji Kotorac had been detained and then ultimately sent into Sarajevo city. Now, whether you were aware of it or not, Mr. Mijanovic, Muslims of Gornji Kotorac were driven out of Ilidza by the Ilidza authorities in co-ordination with the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of the Interior. They did not leave on their own and in an unorganised manner; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You claimed in your statement that the Muslims of Ilidza left on their own in an unorganised manner. The documents I showed you indicated that the Muslims of Gornji Kotorac were expelled by the municipal authorities in Ilidza with assistance and co-ordination from the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Justice; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, may I clarify? The Kasindol Kula and Gornji Kotorac and Vojkovici settlements belonged to that part for which I said that I had never been in during the war physically. That part and those settlements, the decision for temporary accommodation was prepared by the Kasindol war commission and it was brought to me for my signature pro forma as the president in Ilidza. The MUP and the army systems to a considerable extent, as far as I was concerned, were closed systems. And believe me that as far as this eastern part, which is how we referred to it, is concerned, I had no information about anything there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. But were you involved then in resettling Serbs into the -- into empty accommodation in that part of Ilidza, Kasindol and Gornji Kotorac? Were you involved in housing Serbs in Muslim homes there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, by - and I repeat - way of the war commission from those local communes, preparing the forms and proposals for decisions to move in the refugees Serb population into abandoned houses. I would sign that in Ilidza. It would arrive by mail, by messenger, and then I would intensively participate in these matters only in the event of complaints.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You also said in your statement that although the authorities of the Serb municipality of Ilidza maintained contacts with Republika Srpska authorities, you said there were no instructions or orders issued by the authorities and organs of the Republika Srpska to expel or carry out ethnic cleansing of non-Serbs, and that's at paragraph 6 of your statement. On Sunday when we spoke you confirmed that you personally had no contacts with any members of the Republika Srpska authorities, the authorities at the republic level, during the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So although you speak to the nature of those contacts, is it fair to say that you do not have any detailed knowledge about what was discussed or concluded in the contacts that other municipal authorities in Ilidza had with the republic authorities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, for example, you didn't know that Ilidza officials, including Mr. Prstojevic, had a meeting with General Mladic on the 15th of June, 1992, at which it was concluded -- or at which one of the conclusions of the meeting were "to clear the Serbian territory in which Mojmilo and Dobrinja come first." You don't know about that meeting? Reference is P1478, page 170.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I'm concerned, this is the top of the military and political establishment and there was no reason for me to be involved or informed about any of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you also didn't know that ten days after this meeting on the 25th of June, 1992, Mr. Prstojevic had a conversation with Rade Ristic, that Mr. Prstojevic confirmed or referred to Dobrinja 1 and Dobrinja 4, and that was at transcript page 13561, where Mr. Prstojevic instructed Mr. Ristic to hold on to it tightly and have them all killed there, all that is Muslim to be killed like Alija, and that he does not want to see one military-aged Muslim alive there. You don't know about that conversation on the 25th of June, ten days after the meeting with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Rade Ristic is a person from Vojkovici. I don't know exactly what his function was, and in any event that is a part where Prstojevic lived before the war so he maintained those personal contacts. And in any case, he was the kind of person who would not give his associates unnecessary information, particularly not to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So you can't really say then to what extent Mr. Prstojevic's instructions to Mr. Ristic on the 25th of June, 1992, are consistent or inconsistent with the meeting ten days earlier that Mr. Prstojevic and others had with General Mladic and the conclusions drawn at that meeting, can you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comment. I am unable to comment about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And were you aware that in July of 1992, Mr. Prstojevic attended a Republika Srpska Assembly session and said that: "Namely when the Serbs started the uprising in Sarajevo and when they seized control over certain territories there was no government or at least it was not known where it was then. Moreover, we even did not know if Mr. Karadzic was alive during the first couple of days. When we learnt that he was alive and when he visited us in Ilidza and encouraged us, the Serbs from Sarajevo retained control over the territory and even extended their territory in some areas, driving the Muslims out of the territories where they had actually been a majority." Are you aware that Mr. Prstojevic made this speech to the Republika Srpska Assembly in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I thought that Mr. Karadzic throughout the war never went to Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, are you coming to a close?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, I have one last document and one last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd just like to show you one last document, Mr. Mijanovic, which is P1486, page 186. And this document you're about to see is an extract from General Mladic's military notebook from the period 1994 and this entry is from the 6th of July, 1994. And it is a meeting with President Prstojevic, and you've confirmed that Mr. Prstojevic was still the president of Ilidza municipality at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, I don't think we have uploaded the B/C/S version yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And it's at the bottom of the page, meeting with President Prstojevic. And Mr. Prstojevic says: "In connection with the assets confiscated," and we turn to the next page, "from captured Muslims, more than 200.000 German marks was confiscated." And then it lists a number of military items, bullet-proof jackets, Motorola hand-held radios, mine detectors, and it lists the thousands of Deutschemarks for these items. And the last part of this entry says: " ... for the Corps 31.000 Deutschemarks." The last question for you, Mr. Mijanovic, is: Were you aware that Mr. Prstojevic was involved in confiscating 200.000 Deutschemarks from captured Muslims and that he was providing some of these funds to the Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Mark that 31.000 please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few questions, Your Excellencies. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mijanovic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to remind both you and myself to pause between answer and question. Can you please tell me, if you know, whether a prisoner of war has the right to keep his money and valuables? If you don't know this legal matter, then never mind.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a difficult question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that the eastern part of Ilidza was physically separated from the part where you were. How was it separated, this eastern part?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The territory held by, let us call them, federal forces, the Muslim/Croatian forces, that is Dobrinja, Hrasnica, Sokolovic Kolonija, as well as the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And before we surrendered the airport to the United Nations, was there this physical connection, did it exist?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you able to tell us then where the line of confrontation was in relation to Gornji Kotorac, Donji Kotorac, Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija, and Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know because that's the eastern part which was not accessible to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Thank you. In the western part, Sokolovic Kolonija and Hrasnica in relation to the Serbian part of Ilidza, where were the lines of separation there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lines of confrontation were immediately behind the Ilidzanska Aleja Avenue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And according to your knowledge, throughout the war were Gornji Kotorac, Donji Kotorac, Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija, and Hrasnica and the Serb parts of Ilidza part of the Sarajevo front?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to me, the part of Ilidza where I was was constantly a war zone. Literally we did not have a narrow area behind our backs that was safe. Throughout the war there was firing at Ilidza, at the hospital, the schools, and other institutions. Probably in the eastern part Kasindol and the Kasindol hospital were somewhat more protected in that sense. All the other settlements were either along the line of separation or they were constantly exposed to combat action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when Prstojevic is being cited or some other soldier and when it says it will be cleansed, what does that mean to you, cleansing, in military terminology? What is it being cleansed of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, before you answer. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The witness denied all knowledge of all matters military. This is a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We agree, Mr. Karadzic. Move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at P1126 for a moment again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we are waiting, Mr. Mijanovic, can you please tell us if on or around the 12th of May, 1992, there were any events in the Ilidza area, both east and west?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify a little bit? What sort of events?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know when -- do you know if there were any attacks carried out at Ilidza and what were the most intensive attacks from the beginning of April until the end of May in that area?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in April, the 22nd, the 24th, there was a horrendous attack on Ilidza even though I was not in Ilidza at the time. The second and perhaps the largest attack for the whole war period occurred on the 14th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you able to look at this first paragraph here now? Could you please read it in its entirety. Not the information but since May 12th, could you please read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ministry of Internal Affairs, attention president SJB --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, this passage that begins: From the 12th of May ...

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Since the 12th of May, 1992, until the 20th of May, 1992, there are 156 persons detained in KPD Butmir, taken into custody on various grounds. Preliminary operative interviews were conducted with these persons and lists containing all necessary personal data were delivered on time to the MUP Vraca ..." or something like that, out of this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. This is sufficient. This paragraph, does it tell you something and what does this mean "on various grounds"? Were they brought in on a discriminating basis because of their religion or was there any grounds for any kind of criminal acts?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really wouldn't be able to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's all right. The witness answered it. Again, this witness said he had no involvement or any knowledge of these kinds of operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I was about to raise the same point, but the witness has answered. I don't see any point of questions as to which the witness has already answered that he doesn't know. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I don't need to call up document P1151.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was a question put to you in regard of that on page 14, and it was suggested in the question that the -- you were resettling - that was the term that was used. Were you resettling Serbs when you were issuing these decisions or were you doing something else?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no resettling. It was temporary accommodation of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what does that mean, temporary?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means without -- actually, in the decisions that I signed, it is clearly noted that the temporary category means until the end of war at the latest without the person living there acquiring the right of ownership or tenancy in the said accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the property of those who left during the war, Muslims and Croats who left Ilidza, was it returned to the owners in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the information from the post-war period that was available to me, the Republika Srpska area was where all movable property was restored to its rightful owners, ownership of land, property, apartments up to a percentage of 99.9 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question has to do with some intercepts being quoted. Did you understand that these conversations were serious, especially when Prstojevic says: Anybody who takes on the Orthodox faith can stay. How did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Prstojevic is one of the people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Mijanovic. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In light of the witness's answer about having no knowledge of any of the substance of these conversations, I don't think this is a fair question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, agree again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was quoted to you that Serbs from Ilidza controlled some Muslim settlements as well. Can you recall any Muslim neighbourhood that came under our control and can you tell us the main Muslim neighbourhoods and can you tell us whether this was an exaggeration or whether that was correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall any Muslim settlement in particular that was under the control of the Serbian army or the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And after these first battles, were there any Muslims and Croats left in Ilidza? Did they remain to live there? And were there any refugees coming to Ilidza who were not Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any event, there was quite a number of Croats, in view of the fact that the neighbouring Kiseljak was a predominantly Croat settlement, and by the very nature of things the area between Kiseljak and Ilidza was an area where there were a lot of mixed marriages, so that we had the situation where a certain number of Croats were included in the work duty and war time activities on the Serbian side. And there were cases that Serbs in Kiseljak participated in HVO formations or however they were called. As far as Muslims are concerned, there were many more elderly citizens who stayed in Ilidza to guard their apartments or their homes. I could refer to them as non-vital -- the non-vital population. It's true that there were instances when somebody would come from the Federal part to Ilidza - perhaps it was an exception but it was a telling example - the one of Andjelko Raguz, a pre-war policeman who came from the Federal part. He spent the whole war in the police force in Ilidza and he's living in the Serbian part of Ilidza to this day. Probably his reasons for doing that were that he was born and all his forefathers lived in predominantly Serb settlements throughout the war. They had no problems with Serbs. So in his way this was how he decided to participate in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Mijanovic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mijanovic. Now your evidence is over; I thank you on behalf of the Chamber for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we bring the next witness then?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you need a short break, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning. We'll just need to shift. It will only take a couple of minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Ms. Edgerton, I wasn't informed whether or not a Rule 90(E) advice is warranted for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't have my earphones on and I actually didn't hear you. I don't have the transcript in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The answer is yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Indjic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you start giving evidence, Mr. Indjic, I would like to draw your attention to a particular Rule here at the Tribunal. Under this rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the accused, the Prosecution, or from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Indjic. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Like all the witnesses who speak Serbian, I have to ask you and also remind myself for the benefit of the interpreters and the transcript that we should pause between question and answer and answer and question. I see you've been promoted in the transcript to colonel, whereas I said lieutenant-colonel, but that's a good omen.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I would like to thank the court reporter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you ever provided a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to call up 1D7030 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the statement that you gave to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the beginning of the statement, but I would like to be shown the last page to make sure that the entire statement is included.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the last page and the signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is the statement that I gave to your Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read the statement and does it reflect accurately your words?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read the entire statement and it reflects my words accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today that were put to you by members of my team, would your answers to the questions in essence be the same?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: My questions to the -- my answers to these questions would be the same in essence, perhaps somewhat longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender this package, but a number of documents will be led live. From pages 49 through the end of the statement, we will lead this viva voce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you will redact those paragraphs, i.e., para -- from para 173 to para 189?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With that understanding, we'll receive the statement unless there's an objection from Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2774, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I will read out in English a summary statement of Lieutenant-Colonel Milenko Indjic. [In English] Milenko Indjic was a liaison officer in the Main Staff of the SRK. Milenko Indjic was not familiarised with the strategic objectives of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. He considers that the operations were mainly defensive, to maintain the line of separation that had been established when barricades were set up before the war broke out. The blockade of the 1st Corps of the BH army -- the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps prevented 40.000 fighters from this 1st Corps from Sarajevo joined other fronts, which would have given the BH army an important military advantage. It was the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps's commitment that a total cessation of hostilities should take place in BH. An agreement was made in June 1992 that the airport should be taken over by the UNPROFOR and used exclusively for humanitarian purposes. Milenko Indjic had never heard of any plan to completely eliminate the Muslim population of Sarajevo nor to deliberately target the civilian population. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps lacked professional servicemen at lower levels. The means of communication between corps command and brigades functioned well. From brigade level to lower units, a person had to be sent to the location to stop the fire from a weapon, which could take half an hour. There were difficulties with the supply of clothing, ammunition, spare parts, food, and fuel, which was often bought from UNPROFOR members. Lieutenant-Colonel Milenko Indjic states that it was clearly specified in the rules when a unit can open fire without the order of superior command; for instance, if the troops or the buildings which they have possession of are under fire, or there is an activity directly threatening to the lives of the troops. However, issues occurred in lower levels of the soldiers because there were not a sufficient number of professional officers. Daily reports of troop activities were submitted to the corps command as part of the regular procedure. There were a number of paramilitary units in BH and efforts were made to prevent the existence of these units and to place them under the control of corps command. In 1993 these units were disbanded and the individuals reassigned to the units with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The Muslims in B&H adopted the same principles as had been seen in Croatia and Slovenia. They carried out blockades of the JNA barracks, the JNA centres, military hospital, school centres, and barracks of the military police unit. Further, they carried out massacres against the JNA. At the beginning of the war, a large number of civilians of various nationalities were leaving Sarajevo, the VRS was allowing all civilians to leave. The Muslim authorities did not allow both Muslims and Serb civilians to leave. As liaison officer, Lieutenant-Colonel Milenko Indjic's main activity was to co-ordinate all activities of the international institutions with the activities of VRS. The group received requests, protests, and petitions from the other side or representatives of the international community for institutions on their side. These requests were processed and forwarded and vice versa. The PTT building where the group worked was situated in the Muslim-controlled area and frequent firing could be heard. The liaison team moved to Lukavica in mid-September when they received direct threats from the Muslim side that they would be killed. In his role as liaison officer, Milenko Indjic could not give approval of movement of UNPROFOR and humanitarian aid convoys. This could only be given exclusively through written documents of the Main Staff of Army of Republika Srpska and the corps command. At corps level, the Serb side insisted that the repair of gas, water, and electricity infrastructure be conducted on both sides. The Serbs from Ilidza supplied half of Sarajevo. On the other hand the Muslims from Mojmilo did not allow for Lukavica to be supplied. Further uninterrupted communication between Lukavica and Pale was impossible due to the constant fire by the Muslim side. As liaison officer Lieutenant-Colonel Milenko Indjic received protests from UNPROFOR, UNMO, and civilians which he confirmed, dealt with quickly, and passed to the appropriate level. However, a number of these came from the other side and were a war time ploy. Protests lodged by the Serbian side were never given any response. Full satisfaction was expressed by all members of the UN with the level of co-operation received from the SRK, and this was declared openly at meetings. During the fighting in Sarajevo, the BH opened artillery fire on a daily basis from the area of the Kosevo Hospital and other civilian objects. Due to the nature of Sarajevo, the entire city of Sarajevo was at the same time a civilian area and a military area. The Patriotic League entered the war in an organised fashion compared to the Serb side which was only formed at the outbreak of the conflict. Lieutenant-Colonel Milenko Indjic did not receive protests from civilians about shelling emanating from SRK forces. Neither he did receive any protests about deliberate or indiscriminate targeting of civilians. A plan never existed of low intensity operations with the aim of terrorising civilians in Sarajevo. An anti-sniper agreement was drawn up, signed by General Galic; however, this was ineffective. The Serb side allowed humanitarian aid use of the blue routes that had previously been agreed; however, the Muslim leadership refused to let the convoys pass as they were preventing the movement of civilians and making leaving Sarajevo impossible. On one occasion a container for the neighbourhood of Butmir or Dobrinja was searched and weapons and ammunition were found concealed inside. That would be a short summary. Now I would like to pose some questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, two issues. First, I'm not sure if this is a translation issue, but at the end -- at the outset of your summary, although it does not form part of evidence, you introduce Mr. Indjic as a liaison officer in the Main Staff of the SRK. I'm not sure if I understand it correctly. So you clarify with the witness. And secondly, in the case of other military personnel, I would like you to deal with his military career before and after the war as well. Please continue, briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, what did you liaise or who did you liaise between on behalf of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, the institutions and -- the institution and group for co-operation with the international community was specific. It had not existed within the military before that. So physically we were located on the premises of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; however, our work went beyond -- the significance of our work was beyond the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps so that we maintained communication between the Main Staff of the VRS and international organisations and also partly with the political leadership and between the political leadership and international institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that settles that. Now, could you tell us when you were born and where?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I was born in Sarajevo on April 1st, 1957.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you could tell us in the briefest of terms about your educational background.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I completed my primary education and then I went to the aviation academy with the military, and then the aviation technical academy at Rajlovac. Once I completed my programme there I became an officer and I continued my education through specialised training. I went to a language school. I went to an intelligence training college and I took an exam to become a major, which in military terms is the equivalent of an MA. That would be it as far as my education is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How exactly did you move up in terms of your career? What positions did you hold?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: When I first became an officer after completing the military academy, I started serving in Rajlovac as a platoon commander with cadets in the secondary education centre in Rajlovac. I remained in that command position for some years and then I went to the intelligence school. I continued to serve at the academy in Rajlovac as a teacher of intelligence and security and foreign military forces. When the UN mission for the former Yugoslavia was set up, I received orders from the federal secretariat for All People's Defence assigning me as a member of that group for co-operation with the UN headed by General Aksentijevic. When the JNA left Bosnia and Herzegovina, I was reassigned to work in the group for co-operation with international institutions of the VRS. When the war was over I became a member of the 410th Intelligence Centre, and after leaving that institution, I was with the security administration of the General Staff of the VRS until I retired in 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for all of these appointments that you held after Dayton, was there any verification or check that was conducted by the international community?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think I was vetted by the international community. The positions that I was appointed to were not subject to any checks by the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the war found you working in Sarajevo as a JNA officer; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When the JNA withdrew to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, what were the avenues open to you at that point?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I had two or perhaps three options: A, I could relocate with my colleagues from the Rajlovac centre to Belgrade to the academy there and continue my career as a professor; B, I had the option of paying my debt to the Serb people and everybody else in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or rather, Republika Srpska and help defend the Serb people there - and this is what I did; formally, there was also a third possibility which I never even considered, and that was to desert from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hold any command posts before the war during your career?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: That was only after the academy and before I went to the intelligence school when I was platoon commander in the secondary school training centre in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just to go back briefly to something regarding your career, did you receive any awards, commendations, medals, and the like?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I received a number of commendations. During the war I received the mercy cross for humanitarian work in the war by your side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say "by your side," so you got this medal from Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I said "by your side," incidentally it was you in person as the then-president that actually signed the decision to award this medal to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that you did humanitarian work for the sake of the Serbs alone?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: No, I never saw humanitarian work as something that only pertains to one ethnic group. When it came to humanitarian matters, I always took a broad view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I realise the time. Should I go on with my questions or should we perhaps take the break now? I have about 20 documents to go through live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, could you please tell us which of the parties involved in the war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I have a problem. I'm receiving French interpretation in my headset.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, me too. Channel number 6 is the one that you're looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you hearing me in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm hearing you, but I had translation in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably there's some misconnection. I take it it has been sorted out now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you hear me in Serbian now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- yes, I can -- yes, yes, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me see. Could you repeat, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, Lieutenant-Colonel, which of the warring parties at the beginning of the war and until the month of June was controlling the Sarajevo airport?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The Serb side had the airport under its control until the Sarajevo airport was handed over to the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why exactly was the airport handed over to the UN, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: When the agreement was signed on the hand-over of the airport by the UN, the airport was handed over to be used for humanitarian purposes only, so for shipment of humanitarian aid in order to avoid a humanitarian disaster and so that the UN soldiers there received all of the necessary supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the confrontation lines, how far were they from the airport itself?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: You might say that the confrontation lines comprised the airport area. They were right next to the airport's perimeter, on both sides as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on your military knowledge, what were the most dangerous weapons in terms of constituting a threat to airplanes landing and taking off?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: When you talk about airplanes, first and foremost you talk about anti-aircraft weapons because those are the weapons most frequently used to target any incoming airplanes or, indeed, those leaving the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Serb side actually have such weapons available to them at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Serb side did have anti-aircraft weapons; nonetheless, this was one of the provisions that was part of the airport agreement, which implied that the airport should be safe. And that meant that the anti-aircraft weapons had to be moved out of that area and out of range so that they couldn't target any aircraft landing or taking off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D06510. Could that document please be brought up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's a letter that I wrote to the UN. Were you shown this document at any point during proofing and are you familiar with the subject matter?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The Defence team showed me this document so I am familiar with it. As for the subject matter, yes, I'm absolutely familiar with that. I was personally involved in co-ordinating these activities in terms of pulling out the anti-aircraft weapons, in keeping with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to the next page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the principal concern of the Serb side in terms of a plane potentially being shot down?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The principal concern was to prove where the firing came from, where the plane was targeted from. The main thing was to avoid the Serb side being accused of shooting a plane down. That is why everybody was fully ready to remain in keeping with the agreement in terms of pulling out all the anti-aircraft weapons out of range so that no planes could be targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the incident involving an Italian airplane referred to in this document? How far was this plane from our lines and was an attempt made to pin this on us? Can you please look at A.2.: [In English] "The following forces of the Army of the Republika Srpska are stationed within the 45 kilometre radius of the site where the Italian airplane was downed ..."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, this shows where exactly the Serb forces were. I have no accurate information regarding that incident, but there was intelligence that was retrieved after the incident and the whole thing was analysed. I think this was an Italian airplane that was shot down somewhere in the Fojnica general area and I think it was targeted by the Croat forces if memory serves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were the Serbs able at all to shoot down a plane flying over Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please. Can you please go to A.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Any reference to you there in relation to organising the humanitarian nature of the UNHCR flights?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, my name is mentioned there, and I can explain that when the airport was over and fully operational, then there were specially appointed liaison officers whose duty it was to monitor those humanitarian flights at Sarajevo airport and elsewhere, abroad, at Frankfurt, for example. So I ceased to be involved in this, but what we're looking at in this specific case, yes, I was involved and that was my role at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Once the Serb side handed the airport over to UNPROFOR, was the airport used for humanitarian purposes alone or was it also put to other kinds of use?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I assert that the airport was also used for other purposes which we believed to constitute a misuse of the terms. I'm talking about the runway. I'm talking about the area above the runway as well as the area under the runway. The UNPROFOR people knew about the fact that a tunnel was built underneath the airport which the Muslim forces used to regroup. The airport was also used for the transport of Muslim delegations of varying levels for the purposes of their travel across the world and they were lobbying for the Muslim cause. It was also used to bring in persons with assignments that were at the very least suspicious. Neither were they members of diplomatic missions nor indeed were they members of the UN. And the greatest instance of misuse of the airport, the airport was used for the purpose of arming the Muslims. There were several examples of that. The most dramatic example being when ammunition was found hidden in a double-bottomed container that was used to ship humanitarian aid into Butmir airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation and you can also follow on your own screen to make sure interpretation is completed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No objection, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2775, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the whole, what was the position of the Serb side regarding shipment of humanitarian aid for civilians, not just by air but on the whole? What position did the Serb side take to that issue, civilian supplies for Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The Serbian approach, generally speaking, was a positive as far as any form of humanitarian aid was concerned, food, clothes, medical supplies, evacuations. But it was always important to underline and point out the fact that Sarajevo was not just the limited extent of Sarajevo under Muslim control but that Sarajevo was a broader area. And the issue of humanitarian aid was something that should apply equally to all, regardless of ethnicity. People were starving everywhere. In Grbavica which was Serb controlled at the time, in Vogosca which was Serb controlled at the time, just the same as people in Muslim-controlled Sarajevo were starving and were short of food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Was a procedure agreed with UNPROFOR and other international organisations in terms of allowing convoys to pass through and endowing our side with the right to check the convoys coming in?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: There was a war on, so it was necessary to define certain norms and frameworks within which humanitarian convoys were free to move in and out. This had nothing to do with restricting UNPROFOR's freedom of movement because UNPROFOR was there merely to act as an escort for humanitarian convoys. What was the procedure about? Primarily a convoy had to be announced in a timely manner so that we knew exactly when it would be arriving and what route into Sarajevo it would be taking as well as any equipment that they were bringing in. There were two reasons for that, the first being the timely issuance of permits so that the relevant units could receive their orders --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I please ask you to just slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The first reason being orders could be issued in a timely manner to specific units through whose area of responsibility a convoy would be passing, in order to make sure that all of the convoy personnel were fully safe. Secondly, everything being brought in would be checked in order to make sure there was nothing untoward happening, such as military equipment being brought in, which was not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there instances of such abuses?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, what -- how did it work? If a convoy appeared at a check-point without previous announcement and without any declaration on what they were carrying, what would happen?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, in those cases the convoy would not be allowed to pass through our zone and they would be turned back until they submitted the requests that were required and followed the rules and procedure that everyone was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what would happen if a convoy received a permit for Karakaj and they would show up at Sefik?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: They wouldn't be allowed to pass. It would have to follow the requested route and the route that was already approved. And again I have to say this was primarily because the objective was to ensure the safety of the convoy along the axis where it was moving. And we have to bear in mind that the convoys were moving through war zones. It was war time after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at 1D01472, could we pull it up in e-court. 1D01472. Would you please take a look at paragraph 3 which speaks of lack of understanding. Please read it out to yourself and tell us what it deals with.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Here we see in paragraph 3 that there are several elements. The first element deals with Blazuj and a factory in Blazuj and the Orao aircraft factory where UNPROFOR members tried to enter those facilities. I have to clarify something here. These were by no means isolated incidents. It was clear that some elements of the UN had their own intelligence missions and tasks, including establishing what the situation was at certain facilities and locations. That is quite normal and it was quite understandable; however, it couldn't be handled the way anyone wished them to be handled. There had to be approval and agreement, either with the civilian authorities from the area where that particular facility was located or in agreement with military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one question in that respect. The mandate, the UN mandate, that we agreed to, did that include intelligence work without our approval and without our knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The UN mandate, as far as I know, was to provide -- to ensure humanitarian missions and oversee them on the ground, and all activities were supposed to be completely transparent and transparency implies exclusion of any intelligence activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the remainder of paragraph 3, just tell us briefly what it deals with.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The remainder of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have to bear with the interpreters, so please, you should also interfere when I am not on time.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Now, the problems, here it deals with the regular problems that occurred on a regular basis, the movement of UNPROFOR, for which we always tried to ensure the safest routes. And in this particular instance I -- and this was outside of my authorities as the Chief of Staff admonished me, but I took it upon myself to allow this convoy to pass through the zone where the command was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the next page, please. Now I made the error.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: On this page we can see that incident that I mentioned a few moments ago. I'm aware of this instance where a French humanitarian convoy was stopped, and these problems were especially present and difficult with convoys arriving from France. The reason being that Sarajevo had the greatest number of French forces. There was the French Battalion 2 at the airport, 4 at Skenderija, 5 at Hadzici, I believe, so that the French took advantage of the presence of the French troops there and they felt that they didn't really have to comply with the procedures and that they were sufficient, that they could secure their own contingents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the next page in the Serbian version. The English version is fine. What does the first paragraph deal with here? It says there was a misunderstanding, something to do with some containers, and did they have the right to interfere with the deployment of our forces?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, this problem with a container at the entrance to Kasindolska Street, that's also something that I'm also quite familiar with. Kasindolska Street had the following position: The entrance to the street was open to infantry fire from the Muslim side, from Dobrinja. And for this reason, there was a container placed at that spot that was supposed to serve as - if I may put it that way - an anti-sniper barrier. Now, I'm not quite aware what the reason was for UNPROFOR to feel that this container shouldn't be there because it didn't interfere with the traffic at all and there were numerous such containers in various places of Sarajevo that were under Muslim control and there were even instances where the UNPROFOR themselves placed containers for those purposes. So it was our impression that simply they were trying to provoke our reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please read the third paragraph, "It is clear that..." Could you please read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: "It is clear that the UN are mounting an offensive against us, and the considerable amount of arrogance they are displaying is the kind usually meted out to those who have lost a war." It is difficult for me to make any comment here because this kind of behaviour or conduct by a large number of members of the UN was predominant throughout the war and this was the -- their conduct towards the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about their attitude towards the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I've never heard that any Muslims complained of that, and there was very frequently the impression that they were just an extended arm of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2776, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you know as a liaison officer about the meetings between the warring parties and UNPROFOR and what did you know about the topics that was discussed there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: One of the main methods in trying to establish any kind of cease-fire was to hold these meetings of warring parties where UNPROFOR would mediate, and these meetings would be held at all levels, at General Staff levels, corps commands and even at lower levels. Our general position on this was, in view of the fact that our position from the outside was one of peace, so our position was that we should always accept these meetings and be as constructive as possible in seeking arrangements to stop the conflict. Now, in addition to these arrangements that were supposed to lead to an end to conflicts, there were other -- there was a series of meetings at lower levels where daily problems were discussed, such as humanitarian aid, repairs to infrastructure, such as water-supply, electric supply, medical evacuations, exchanges of prisoners of war, and generally the issue of the freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you attend such meetings and did you have any other authority in addition to your liaison function?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: For the most part, I did attend those meetings, or rather, it would be either me or someone else from the group for co-operation with the UN. Our job was most usually the help as liaison officers, so providing help as liaison officers, perhaps providing interpretation, sending reports or submitting reports. And in some rare instances I was empowered by the commander to sign off on an agreement that had been reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D06513 in e-court, 1D06513. I'm afraid we don't have a translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I will ask you to clarify some of the circumstances there. Can you tell us what this document is about and who is submitting this report, because we see that the Serb delegation is referred to as the Chetnik delegation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before the witness answers, Your Honour, I note that there's no translation of this document, so unless one is expected or undertaken to be provided before the cross-examination begins, I don't know how we can effectively use this document at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were occasions where both sides submitted documents from time to time that hadn't been translated yet, because for us it's also a problem when a document is presented in the English version without a translation. And that is the reason, in fact, why we tried to interpret live these untranslated documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't remember there are many instances the Prosecution used untranslated translation, and I will not comment on your submission that -- regarding the English document. But, Ms. Edgerton, if the Defence is going to use an untranslated document and if the Defence is to introduce the crux of the document, would there be any problem for your preparation? There was such instances before, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And normally I wouldn't rise on something like that if the document was, frankly, rather small. But by my count this document is in excess of ten pages. So if it's something where I thought we could reasonably deal with the crux of the document, by all means, you're absolutely correct. But I think this one which, just by my understanding of some of the citations looks like a transcript of a meeting, is really a bit too big to be able to do that effectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's see whether we can admit this document after his examination on this issue is over.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see where the source of misunderstanding is because my words were misunderstood. On page 47 I said that the reason why we are offering untranslated documents live, although that is not in keeping with the decision of the Trial Chamber, is that they have not been translated. We don't have them. And I don't know what's happening today, but the interpretation is a disaster. It would be simpler to say that it's the position of the Trial Chamber that whatever has not the been translated has to be led live with the witness. That is my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Lieutenant-Colonel, this meeting of the subcommittee held at the airport on the 31st of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I do remember it. There were various subcommittees established to deal with various issues and this is one such subcommittee that was supposed to deal with the issue of ensuring freedom of movement into and out of Sarajevo. This specific document that I see before me is obviously a document produced by the Muslim side, seeing that the delegation that I was a member of was referred to as the delegation of Chetniks, which was not UNPROFOR terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go to page 5 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm the remark made by Ms. Edgerton, this is some sort of a transcript or minutes of that meeting? You see that there are quotes there.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a textbook transcript produced by the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us about this bit from Valentin and then down from there? What is that about? What routes are mentioned and who are these routes for? What is the position of the Serbs? What is that of the Croats? And what is that of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The position of the Serb side in terms of freedom of movement was that freedom of movement had to be ensured unconditionally and had to apply to all. Any restrictions on the freedom of movement in any shape or form would have led to families being torn asunder and to violations of the fundamental human rights of individual persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is the position taken by Mr. Pelko, a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Pelko at the time was the Muslim brigade commander. He took the view that men of military age - that means aged between 16 and 60 - should not be subject to this agreement. A state of war had been declared throughout the Muslim-controlled territory and they refused to allow freedom of movement for all. What this implied was that Serbs would not be allowed to enjoy freedom of movement and would therefore be forced to stay as hostages in Sarajevo because they were not assigned to military units as soldiers, so their only purpose would have been to remain there as hostages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And what was the position taken by the Serb side or, as the document says, the Chetniks, headed by you at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Our position was freedom of movement for all unconditionally, a fundamental human right to choose a place of residence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is some sort of a compromise there. What was the position taken by the UN, by Valentin?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel Valentin was obviously not in a mood to clash with the Muslims there; therefore, he threw out our proposal on freedom of movement for all. Our side then attempted to come up with a compromise. There were those groups that the Muslims wished to deny freedom of movement and we wanted to have this allowed for them based on the principle of reciprocity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please read out what you said at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: A compromise. Stick with unrestricted freedom of movement but without having a regrouping of military forces, that is, that for men aged between 16 and 60 and for them to enjoy freedom of movement based on the principle of reciprocity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please focus on the part about Valentin and Srebrenica. And then what is Pelko saying, what are you saying, and what is Valentin saying there?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we pull up the page, please. Thank you. Thank you. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So after where it says "in Srebrenica" and then on from there.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: It is quite obvious what the position is taken by the UN and the Serb side is the same thing.
