No separation of families must be allowed, despite which the Muslim side here invokes the fact that they have a state of war in their territory and that men are military conscripts and they refuse to have unconditional freedom of movement as part of this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please read what Pelko says, where he says "we are sticking with," and on from there. Take it easy, please. One quote at a time.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: "Pelko: We are sticking with women, children aged up to 16, and men aged up to 60 under international law. This is a war and military conscripts must stay or men liable to military duty must stay. "Valentin: This is not an international law. This is a rule that we are imposing ourselves. Here are the conclusions based on my proposal because these are humanitarian corridors. "Indjic: We accept the compromise to keep the families together and for the men to be released."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 8 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please read your own quote, your own contribution, where you say "I cannot understand."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: My quote: "I cannot understand why we can't go for unconditional freedom because we are offering to others the same thing that we are claiming for ourselves."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please just look at another page, page 3 -- or actually, just a minute, please. We have ERN 084. Page 3 it is. Can you please tell us what this is about. They're talking about collection centres. "Valentin: What would be a good places for a collection centre?" And then what are the Chetniks saying and then all the way up to Pelko's contribution.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: This is about technical issues, where to organise collection points for people and what routes would be used in order to possibly implement this agreement concerning freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then about Dobrinja, Valentin is asking about Dobrinja. What is Pelko saying in response to that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: He says that it would not be a good idea to assemble anywhere that close to the front line. In my opinion, this is a paradox. You had front lines all over Sarajevo so there was no place that was safe from a front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Unlike this assembling that was announced, how did you view the football matches that were happening close to the collection point in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Obviously each of the positions were made to fit respective needs. Whenever there was no need for political or media manipulation, whenever there was no need to avoid a certain agreement, then Dobrinja was no good. But when one had to organise a football match then the exact location of a front line did not matter at all and it proved to be, after all, a perfectly appropriate location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please tender this for identification until a complete translation of this document is received. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have no problem with it being marked for identification pending translation and further submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D2777, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to note I think Ms. Edgerton made that note indicating further submissions, but in the past sometimes we've admitted documents MFI simply pending the translation because of a full understanding of what the document was about. In this case and I believe in some of the future matters, the MFI also includes the possibility of examining the document and then determining whether or not further submissions are necessary regarding admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your point is taken. Before we take away this document, it's not related to any subject matter, but, Mr. Indjic, how shall we spell your last name in Latin? Is it -- I saw here I-n-d-z-i-c, but I was also looking at your statement, which writes -- which reads as I-n-d-j-i-c.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the spelling in this document is inaccurate. It's the other spelling that you mentioned that is actually correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D06522 brought up in e-court. To see what UNPROFOR had to say about this same meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the same meeting of the joint military working group on the 31st of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please read item 2 and tell us whether you believe UNPROFOR understood your position properly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where it says "Serbs" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, did you say this is an UNPROFOR document? And we have no English version. Is it the case, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We couldn't track one down, but yes it's an UNPROFOR report. There must be an original, but I was unable to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So since you are not giving evidence yourself, I would like to hear the confirmation from the witness. In the future you should ask the question to the witness to confirm your submission. Do you confirm that, Mr. Indjic, this is an UNPROFOR document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's obvious if you look at the header. It's an UNPROFOR document. After each meeting all of the parties involved would receive a translation of the minutes by UNPROFOR to keep for their own files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic. Just a second. Yes, Mr. Indjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to answer because I heard Mr. Karadzic's question so I might as well answer it. In item 2 UNPROFOR reflects the position taken by the Serbs. It reads: "The Serbs will not have any restrictions. Everyone is to be allowed to move about freely."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Was UNPROFOR's interpretation of the position you took at that meeting correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document, or rather, have it marked for identification, same as the previous one? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D2778, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you not have English version in your possession, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I'd been aware of one, I would have offered it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, during your liaison activity, did you receive any information about the fighting in 1993, specifically around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: What I can remember is that I was, I believe, accompanying General Mladic at a meeting with, I believe -- perhaps it was General Milovanovic. It was one of these two, someone from the Main Staff. At this meeting the fighting around Srebrenica at that time was referenced, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any meetings that you attended and who were the negotiating parties involved?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I think it was this mixed or joint military group and there was an attempt being made to have a cease-fire agreed for all of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what positions were taken by the opposing parties, or rather, the warring parties on the one hand and the mediators on the other, specifically about Srebrenica and about the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The position taken by the Serb side, generally speaking, was that Bosnia-Herzegovina in its entirety was affected by war and that it wasn't appropriate to talk about small-scale cease-fires that only applied to certain limited areas. Given the overall situation, war raging across the country. The Muslim side already had, in manner of speaking, Srebrenica in its sights back then and tried to get maximum media exposure for what was going on there so the media were trying to show that everything that was going on there at the time had been planned a long time ahead. As a matter of principle the Croats would never put forward anything at all at any of the meetings. They would always agree with the chairperson but every time a meeting was over, they just continue doing their own thing, promoting their own agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber why the Serb side deemed it unacceptable or why was it more acceptable to have a cessation of hostilities or a cease-fire throughout all of Bosnia and why did the Muslims, on the other hand, deem it more appropriate or more acceptable to have limited extent of cease-fires in particular areas that they found convenient?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: We're talking about 1993. No state of war had been declared in Republika Srpska. Why? By doing that, we clearly demonstrated our own position. We did not want a war. We did not want cease-fires. We wanted for the war to end and for all hostilities to cease throughout the territory. That would have put an end to the war. As for limited extent, small-scale cease-fires, in our view that would not have contributed to ending the war but rather to drawing the whole thing out and prolonging the situation and that would also help some forces to consolidate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who exactly?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, those requesting such cease-fires. Specifically we're talking about Srebrenica, in that case we're referring to the Muslim forces there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a 1D20177 in e-court, please. There is a translation available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, please have a look. Were you shown this document during proofing? And can you briefly tell us what the document is about?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was shown this document during proofing. I remember the meeting. It's one of the meetings, high-level meetings, the only such high-level meeting that was held in the presence of delegations from Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The principal purpose of this meeting was to try and find a way to put an end to hostilities throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I want to know about an assertion made there by General Milovanovic. It's line 2, General Milovanovic is quoted as saying: "General Milovanovic told him that the cease-fire is already costing us over 50.000 [as interpreted] dead and that there should be a cease-fire throughout the theatre of war. How come there is a cease-fire on and still so many lives are lost?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The corps conducted some analysis showing that the greatest losses were suffered -- occurred during cease-fires because people took some agreements at face value, and as a result they would relax. And then the other side violated the cease-fire as a result of which we suffered casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What exactly did you know about these cease-fire violations?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: That depended on the level at which cease-fires were agreed and whether there were groups organised to monitor the implementation of cease-fires. So any insight I had into these violations depended on these circumstances. From personal experience I can say that I do not remember a single agreed cease-fire that was fully complied with throughout the agreed time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in from -- notice and protests with respect to violations of cease-fires, would they be sent through you as the liaison officer? Or were they sent directly by fax to the addressees?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, here I have to make a distinction. There were different levels and there were two periods. At first, in the first period, the only office of the liaison officer that was active was in Lukavica and most of the correspondence went through that office in Lukavica. However, very soon after that - and I believe that this was in late 1993 - UNPROFOR established their own liaison office at Pale so that the communications went from that office, the communications that related to the Main Staff. In other words, they didn't go through the office at Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The violations of cease-fires in Sarajevo, was that something that you had more insight into if they didn't go toward the Main Staff, but rather brigades and corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part yes because it was our duty to take excerpts from daily combat reports that related to cease-fires. We were supposed to reformulate them and inform the UNPROFOR command thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the response of the UNPROFOR command when we lodged our protests?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: We seldom had any response.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just related to that document, before we go too far in the transcript, there's a citation at page 59, lines 8 and 9, and Dr. Karadzic says at line 2 General Milovanovic is quoted as saying something to the effect of the cease-fire had already cost us over 50.000 dead. And I don't see that anywhere in the document or my translation of the document. So I wonder if there should be a transcript correction or what Dr. Karadzic was actually quoting. It could be my oversight, but just to make the inquiry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 2, toward the top of the page in Serbian I said -- and I read out. Here, we can see it here and I will read it out now: "General Milovanovic told us that so far we've had over 50 dead as a result of this cease-fire ..." And if the transcript does not reflect that, the document does. That's paragraph 3 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but the transcript said "50.000." Thank you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2779, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, can you tell us were there any attempts to demilitarise Sarajevo and what were the positions of the warring parties, especially the Serbian and the Muslim sides on demilitarisation of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, our general position was that a demilitarisation of Sarajevo would be a great contribution to putting an end to the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and especially that it would -- that it would provide for a far smaller number of casualties. Now, the demilitarisation of Sarajevo was something that was always mentioned by the Serb side and one of the specific examples, such examples, was the meeting at the Sarajevo airport following a resolution by the UN that -- whereby the protected areas of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde were established, which lasted about 48 hours, the meeting, and at this meeting General Mladic pleaded that Sarajevo be included in that agreement so that the war could be stopped. However, these proposals were never accepted by the Muslim side because it was clear that a possible demilitarisation of Sarajevo would mean an end to the war and that Sarajevo as the martyr town was very important for the Muslims in this war. And whoever it was who decided when the war -- who could decide when the war would end did not allow this issue to be discussed. To me it would have been far more useful to demilitarise Sarajevo rather than Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now pull up 1D6520 in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you recall this meeting, Lieutenant-Colonel, and could you tell us who attended the meeting on behalf of the VRS? You can see that under "participants."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I see that this was a meeting of the joint military group. I already explained that this was at the General Staff level and we can see that on the Serb side it was attended by General Gvero, Colonel Tolimir at the time, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the Muslim and Croatian sides?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: It was Colonel Divjak on behalf of the Muslims and Mr. Muslimovic and the commander of the 4th Military Group on behalf of the Croatians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please just take a look at this. We don't have to read this out. Your English is good enough. Can you just tell us what the first and second paragraphs deal with.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, I'm not sure if we are receiving the translation. Could you kindly repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've said, we can see from this document that the parties had an interest to declare Sarajevo a safe area. I'm not going to go through the whole document, but I do know what the basic distinction in the approaches of the various parties was. The Muslim party insisted on pulling out artillery outside Sarajevo, whereas they themselves were not prepared to demilitarise their own infantry in Sarajevo. So these were two quite contradictory positions that could not lead, that were not conducive to any kind of solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please read out the comment here on the Serb interests, the comment by the UN, and is this a -- an accurate reflection of what the Serb side advocated at that meeting? It's toward the centre of the page.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that comment and this is a fair assessment of both parties, the positions of both parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2780, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, did you attend meetings or were you aware of any meetings in the course of 1994 where the removal of heavy weapons was discussed, the removal of heavy weapons from the town itself?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I did attend a number of such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, what was in effect the essence of these agreements?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The essence of the agreement on the grouping of heavy weapons was to provide the basic conditions for long-term cease-fire in the Sarajevo region. An additional protocol to the agreement on the control of weapons implied the cessation of all other combat activities in this period.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we kindly ask that the witness move back from the microphone a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, could you kindly move back from the microphone a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to mention the Prosecution document P2120 which is a document dealing with the agreement on the grouping of heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, was this grouping of heavy weapons ever implemented as agreed? Were they grouped in these five areas that were mentioned here? We can see that there were five of them mentioned, they were Lukavica, Mokro, Blagovac, Blazuj and Radava?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the weapons, artillery weapons, were grouped in these locations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have Exhibit P1641 for just a brief moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I would like to ask you to explain a position there of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Please take a look at paragraph 1 that deals with -- actually, it's a proposal to extricate artillery and then there's a proposal to the Main Staff. Could you please just read out the first paragraph. Read it to yourself and then tell us what it deals with.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I quote: "With the aim of issuing a decision and giving an approval for the procedure of setting aside artillery according to the request of UNPROFOR, we are sending you the proposal that we consider to be a solution and which enables promptness in work. Upon the implementation of this proposal, the SRK forces would not suffer any damages and would not be left without equipment since we would use a diversionary tactic to set aside the equipment that is out of order and for which we do not have sufficient quantities of ammunition."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, please tell us, what was it that prompted the author of this proposal, General Milosevic, to come up with this kind of proposal. What was the reason for this caution on his part?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, we can see that this is a document from February 1994, so we've already had two years of war behind us. There were numerous violations of various agreements which led to an atmosphere of suspiciousness towards the other party. Now, this proposal, in fact, seeks to avoid a fair implementation of the agreement. And the purpose of that or the objective would be to avoid decreasing the combat-readiness of the VRS in case it was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What date do we see on this document and is it correct that the agreement had been reached on the 16th, or rather, 18th of February, 1994? In other words, did this proposal come before the agreement itself?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that with certainty. I have to see that document -- I have to see the agreement and the date on it. I see that the date on this document is 10 February, but I cannot really recall on what day the agreement itself was reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While we still have this document here, can I ask you was this proposal by General Milosevic accepted and implemented?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I know that it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were his concerns founded and what -- on what were they founded? What was the basis for them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: As I've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps the question could be rephrased because I don't see how, based on this, the witness is able to read General Milosevic's mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably -- is the objection related to the last part of the question what are the -- what was the basis for them?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I can rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My understanding was Mr. Milosevic -- Mr. Karadzic was asking the reason for the refusal. Probably you can rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. First I asked whether and on the basis of what, or rather, what the reasons were for the caution on the part of General Milovanovic and whether life actually showed that this was founded, that his concern was founded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can answer. As I've already said, these were conditions where there was general lack of confidence. That's number one. Number two, the balance of forces in the Sarajevo theatre was maintained because the VRS, or the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, had an advantage in artillery, whereas the Muslim side had an advantage in infantry. Now, placing the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps under control would bring us into a weaker position vis-à-vis the Muslim side. Now that this concern was justified, we can see from the fact that the war continued long after this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. P2120 says the 16th of February and I believe that the agreement was only signed on the 17th or the 18th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't know if we're moving on to another document now, Your Honours, but I just feel I should put on the record that this document which we're discussing, P1641, wasn't even a belatedly notified document. That's a brand new document that has been brought up in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document has been admitted. However, I failed to notify the Prosecution, but this has been admitted as one of their documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the fact that the document was admitted earlier on has nothing to do with your obligation to notify the Prosecution of your usage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but believe me the pace is frantic and it's difficult to keep up with everything, as you can see. Is it sufficient for everyone else involved for me to say that P2120 dated the 16th, so 16 days after this proposal, although the agreement was signed on the 17th or possibly 18th of February. That is for the purposes of orientation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can move on. It's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, are you familiar with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Dr. Karadzic. There's just one thing I wanted to clarify with the witness. Colonel, you said earlier that the Muslims had an advantage in infantry. By that do you mean a numerical advantage or an advantage by -- for other means, such as better weaponry? Better training? Or was it a mixture of both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Numerical advantage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I press on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, were you familiar with the progress of the negotiations and how all these things were being implemented regarding the exclusion area, the total exclusion area within a radius of 20 kilometres surrounding the city for heavy weapons and artillery?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the delegation doing the negotiations and was personally in charge of co-ordinating activities regarding the grouping of these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were the Muslims too under an obligation to comply with this 20-kilometre radius surrounding the city itself and therefore to pull out all of their heavy weaponry from that area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the other side was also under an obligation to comply with that. Nonetheless, we must keep in mind Sarajevo's peculiar configuration. The lie of the land there means that in the built-up parts of Sarajevo they had no place that they could leave those weapons and still remain in keeping with the parameter, the radius. So they had to take those heavy weapons to Butmir and Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the grouping of weapons. And what about weapons being removed from the 20-kilometre radius, was that also a commitment that they undertook under the terms of that particular agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that also applied to the commitment they undertook to pull out the heavy weapons. If we're talking about a 20-kilometre radius that means there are no heavy weapons left in Sarajevo itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the Muslim side acting in keeping with this agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Everything that happened in the war later on and the use of artillery at a later stage in the conflict by the Muslim side clearly demonstrates that they failed to comply with the terms of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about any violations of that agreement that was reached by the Muslims? How did the Serb side respond? What could they do by way of response?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, sir. I don't think I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see for yourself that the Muslims indeed were violating this agreement and what did the Serbs do by way of response?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: We could raise objections with the UNPROFOR command because of this non-compliance, but our own artillery weapons had been pulled out and we couldn't reply in kind, so to speak. Nevertheless, we used what was available to fire back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did UNPROFOR respond to these violations and to your own objections?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: In my personal view, UNPROFOR had very few resources that they could actually use and, indeed, very little authority to impose in order to keep these violations from occurring. So their role basically boiled down to conveying our information to the other side in terms of simple feedback. That was the extent of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was the position taken by the Main Staff of the VRS and the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in terms of our relations with UNPROFOR and in terms of incidents occurring between our soldiers and UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I have to say, we were not too happy to have UNPROFOR there. Our impression from the outset was that they were siding with the other party. Nevertheless, we undertook a professional commitment to build up relations with UNPROFOR at all levels that were nothing but fair and proper. Our foremost priority was to ensure the safety of UNPROFOR. If there were any incidents that left UNPROFOR soldiers at risk, such incidents would invariably be immediately investigated and any perpetrators were punished.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D06518, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if it is convenient, shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll take no more than two minutes to deal with this document. Perhaps it might be a good idea to do that before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D06518, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us about this document, what is it about and tell us in your own words. One look should be sufficient for you to see what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: This is a daily combat report. When there are combat operations going on there would be several such reports submitted each day. We see that this is exactly such a period. There were several such daily reports because, you see, that reflected in the heading their situation at 1700 hours. So one of the elements included in these reports was about the situation on the ground and one of the mandatory features would be a description of UNPROFOR activities. So based on this we see that the military observers are still outside the technical repair centre in Hadzici. So this is not what I was alluding to at the beginning of my evidence today. It's not -- what I mean when I was talking about the intelligence activities pursued by certain UNPROFOR members, or indeed their attempts to gain entry to certain facilities that had not been previously agreed. And then if you go to paragraph 2 you see a description of -- a communication between General Soubirou and myself. Unfortunately I have to say that this was a highly unpleasant situation because I was treated in an exceptionally unprofessional manner by a French general who hated me because I had shown him up for what he was in terms of his role in the tunnel being dug underneath the Sarajevo airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 2, please, there was something exceptional that happened at about 1725. That's paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: This paragraph reflects -- is an incident that occurred involving a soldier who for unknown reasons activated a grenade in the physical proximity to UNPROFOR soldiers. So this person was now being brought in and questioned. That is the soldier who put the lives of UNPROFOR members at risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you give us a brief assessment. You talked about how General Soubirou treated you. How would you generally assess his treatment of the Serb side and do you think his impartiality was affected?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: What I'm offering here is my private opinion based, however, on my knowledge of his actions at the time. I think the things he did were unprofessional. I think he was not neutral and had a definite bias in favour of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you can just tell us what this is about where it says cease-fire related duties.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I do have to give you a breakdown of this for -- on this for you to understand. It's about engineering work. The greatest problem that we faced during cease-fires was the fact that the Muslim forces used these reprieves to take territory by means of engineering work. They would simply gain ground on us by using their engineering people, and because a cease-fire was on we couldn't prevent them from doing that by opening fire. We kept raising this with UNPROFOR, pleading with them to put a stop to that kind of activity; however, to no avail. UNPROFOR did nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I would like to tender this document for admission and then we must take our break. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D2781, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, before we break, I have a brief question for you which is about the accused's motion for safe conduct for General Vasiljevic. The motion does not provide the witness's country of residence. I wonder whether you can inform the Chamber of the country where he currently resides in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break for half an hour -- no, I'm sorry, for three-quarters of an hour and resume at 20 past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, did you know anything about sniping and the charges for sniping of civilians? What was the position of the Serb side in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: For clarification I need to say - and that is also in the statement that was admitted into evidence, in my statement - now, if all of those cases of sniping deaths were taken as being true, then there wouldn't have been any other casualties in Sarajevo other than casualties of sniping. So first of all, as a professional, military professional, I have to say that one can state that had there been sniping and had someone been hit by a sniper rifle bullet, there would have to be a medical examination in order to establish whether the bullet was actually a sniper bullet or not because that kind of bullet is different in weight to the regular bullet. Now, I mention this because all infantry fire was referred to as sniping. Now, accepting -- even if we were to accept the misunderstanding and the misconceptions about sniping, the Serb side was always -- always expressed its readiness to come to any agreement that would lead to a cease-fire, including an agreement on sniping that would actually make sniping impossible by either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any attempts to limit or confine sniping activities outside of this general agreement on a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: There were requests and calls for a separate agreement on sniping, irrespective of a cessation of hostilities or cease-fire agreements, a special agreement that would totally exclude sniping because sniping in key locations was the greatest threat to the civilian population on either side and this is the reason why many anti-sniping obstacles were placed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the position of the Serb side on such agreements? Was it in favour or against and was it in favour of compliance with such agreements?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Our position was clear. We were absolutely in favour of such agreements, primarily because that would have worked in our favour, because sniping was, and this is certain, primarily used by the Muslim side and abused as well. When I say "abused," I can clarify the role of the Seva [phoen] group and the killings of UNPROFOR members as well as one's own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say for the most part used by the Muslim side, could you please explain that because there is a perception here that the Serbs were on the hills and the Muslims were in a subordinate position. So how did that work in terms of sniping activities?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the easiest way to understand this is to provide you some examples. I will give you the example of the crossing at the Mis store on Grbavica 1 -- in Grbavica 1 settlement. I can say that at least 20 civilians were hit at that crossing by a sniper that was from a building on the Muslim side of the town. The second example is the killing of civilians near the national museum, near the Holiday Inn hotel, where a container for -- as a protection against sniping was placed. This example was so obvious because the soldier had been hit from -- laterally, in other words, from the side that was under the control of the Muslims. But nevertheless, the Serb side was automatically accused of this incident as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this or other sniping activities against UNPROFOR members, were they ever investigated and was it ever established and clarified who the culprit was?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately there is a dual situation, as it were, here. After certain incidents thanks to our preparedness and readiness to allow an inspection of our positions, for instance, in the situation where this French soldier was killed, there were two UNPROFOR commissions that came and I went to this infamous red building at Grbavica together with them on two occasions, and we went through every room of the building and we tried to establish where the firing could have come from in respect of or in relation to the direction where the killing occurred. We looked at all the holes from which the firing could have been, and it was established by both these commissions that it couldn't -- that the fire could not have come from the Serb side, but then three days later the Serbs were accused of that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the position of the Serb side on investigations to be conducted by UNPROFOR or the other party and also on the request that the Serb part also participate in investigations that were in the area under the control of the BiH?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, aware of the fact that we were declared the bad guys from the very start, our position was that we should co-operate to the best of our abilities and to allow investigations whenever there was a request for an investigation. Now, as for major disasters, I can't call them incidents, but the major disasters, such as Markale I and Markale II, the Serb side was immediately ready to have Joint Commissions established in order to determine what exactly had happened. And generally our requests in that respect were refused, declined, because they claimed that they could not guarantee for the safety of the members of that commission -- those commissions, but in fact the true reason was that they did not want the truth to come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please pull up in e-court 65 ter 09658. 65 ter 09658.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see your name here and are you aware of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see this. This is a document relating to continued implementation of the measures arising from the anti-sniping agreement that had been signed, and it implied that there should be a liaison group established that would include the so-called BH army, the VRS, and the UNPROFOR, that could then respond to any sniping activities quickly. But as far as I can recall, such a group was never established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything, Lieutenant-Colonel, about why this never materialised, which side was blocking it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I believe that the Muslim side was not ready to send its own representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2782, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, do you remember our withdrawal from Bjelasnica and Igman that had been captured previously and do you know what the regime that was put in place at Igman and Bjelasnica was after that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I remember that very well. I participated in the negotiations at the Sarajevo airport personally and General Milovanovic headed our delegation and signed the agreement on the demilitarisation of the areas of Igman and Bjelasnica, Mounts Igman and Bjelasnica. Now, this agreement was, in fact, provoked by the Muslim side because they wanted to prevent their total collapse because the Army of Republika Srpska was some 100 metres away from the point where the link-up forces from Hadzici and Krupa would be. However, this agreement was not implemented or complied with by the Muslims. In other words, the area was not demilitarised. The French battalion that was at the airport was responsible for the control of that area and they were supposed to oversee the implementation of the agreement; however, that had never happened. And thanks to the fact that there was no demilitarisation, one of the greatest crimes by the Muslim side was committed because they used this unprotected, undemilitarised area to attack a position of the VRS where -- and they killed on that occasion 20 VRS soldiers, of whom four were unarmed nurses. All these people were killed in their sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was the demilitarisation and when did this crime occur?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, it's hard for me to recall this as I sit here, the exact date, but it's quite certain that this crime occurred after the period when the demilitarisation was supposed to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D06521, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know this document? Did you see it at the time or have you seen it perhaps during proofing and what does it deal with?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I was shown this document during proofing and -- but I'm aware of the events described there. The chronology here speaks of our communications between the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the French Battalion, Battalion 5, who were controlling the Igman and Bjelasnica areas for the purpose of the final demilitarisation of that area. It is clear from this document that members of the French battalion -- battalions are being warned that Muslim forces are carrying out combat operations from the zone that was supposed to be demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At 9.40 here we see that the liaison officer reports that there is several casualties. And then can we see your name in the first couple of paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. The entire communication, actually, is a reference to my actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the penultimate paragraph, 1435, what does it say there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, it says here that the Chief of Staff confirms that there are 20 bodies and that some of them were mutilated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mutilated?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, mutilated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that UNPROFOR actually checked your reports and is this what they found?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. This is the Chief of Staff of the UNPROFOR command and this is what they have -- after they have verified our reports. And there is also, I believe, a video-clip entitled Catlaj [phoen], some 20 minutes long, which shows the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say further or could you tell us how these people were killed and by what?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, most of them had their throats slit or were killed with some other cold weapon such as an axe or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did UNPROFOR do after they verified that this crime had actually been committed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Personally, I don't know that any measures were taken against the Muslim side by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2783, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, can you tell us how our withdrawal and the abuse of that withdrawal reflected on the situation among our people and specifically within the ranks of our army?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: There was a pronounced lack of trust and the war was dragging on. For that reason, our withdrawal was seen by most people as a form of defeat. People failed to accept this for what it was. Nonetheless, there was certain agreements that were signed. It was no matter for any of us to personally agree or disagree. These simply had to be complied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What about the Muslim side, did they ever all together leave the area which they were never supposed to take in the first place once it was handed over to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: According to my intelligence, the Bjelasnica and Igman areas were never fully demilitarised by the end of the war, which means that the agreement had not been complied with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D060515. 1D06515.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Chamber who produced this document and what is this about?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The header shows that this is a BH army document, specifically the 1st Corps command, minutes from a meeting held at the airport, a meeting with the Serb side which they refer to here as the Chetniks, so obviously it's not the Croats that we're looking at here. Attending the meeting were Cedo Sladoje, chief of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, Chief of Staff, and myself. It was about the implementation of the demilitarisation agreement of the Igman and Bjelasnica areas. The document clearly shows that the demilitarisation process was not fully implemented by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're talking about January 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, specifically the 5th of January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May this please be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2784, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know about the position taken by the president of the republic, that means me at the time, regarding the passage of humanitarian convoys en route for Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The position taken was perfectly clear if you consider everything that was going on across the area. I never personally heard anything from you on that count, but it was perfectly clear. There was always the demand that nobody should try and stand in the way of humanitarian aid being shipped to civilians. One had to make sure it got there. So we had a whole number of these organisations, Merhamet, Caritas, Dobritor [phoen]. These were humanitarian organisations and they were assisted in every way in their efforts to deliver aid to civilians. There was even the need for co-ordination, obviously, so a special headquarters was set up to help these civilians with regard to the humanitarian situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who on my behalf or on behalf of the Presidency dealt with the issue of humanitarian convoys and co-operation with these humanitarian institutions ensuring safe passage for the convoys?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I think if memory serves it was the late Nikola Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Given the fact that convoys would sometimes pass through several times unhampered, what was the role played by the Main Staff of the VRS in terms of approving these convoys?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: As I said earlier on, the role played by the Main Staff was quite significant because there were procedures in place when approval was granted for each of the convoys and when appropriate checks were made because these convoys were passing through the theatre of war, where combat operations were underway. I explained all these procedures in one of my previous replies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D06516, please. In e-court. Thank you. 1D06516. Unfortunately, the translation of this document has not been completed yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who produced this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please scroll down to the bottom of the page in order to see that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It bears my signature. Having received a request for a convoy to be allowed through, I submitted this request to the Main Staff for approval, proposing also that the convoy should be allowed to pass and that approval should be granted for the 15th of November, 1994. And what follows is your own reply. At my level, I didn't have the authority to approve this or, indeed, to ban this convoy from passing through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to paragraph 1. Who submitted or who had sent the request that you asked for the Main Staff to approve?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph you see that the request came from you, and then based on an agreement that was reached by you and Mr. Akashi, approval was to be granted for general supplies convoy to be approved for Kakanj, specifically the Catholic school there and the canteen. It was about furniture being shipped to that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this be MFI'd, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D2785, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If my colleague Mr. Reid can release 65 ter number 24459, that's a document that I was fortunately able to have translated overnight, as I wasn't able to read it. And I would have risen earlier, Your Honours, and my apologies. I wasn't able to locate that in my e-mails until this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then would you agree that this document would be admitted in full?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That will be done. Thank you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you on behalf of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, given your post, were you in a position to follow the cease-fire negotiations? Were there any cease-fire agreements reached between the Serbs and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Cease-fire agreements were frequently signed. Essentially one of the responsibilities included going through the liaison officers HQ in order to analyse these cease-fire agreements and forward the results of our analysis to both UNPROFOR and the other side in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the fate of such agreements? Did they ever take effect and how long were they complied with?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Based on my recollection, which is what I said earlier on, none of these agreements were actually complied with by the dead-line set out in the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. 65 ter 15433 in e-court, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you personally play a role in the -- any of the follow-ups to these agreements and the implementation of these agreements?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I see a document by the Main Staff of the VRS on the screen, ordering a total cease-fire, a cessation of all hostilities, pursuant to an agreement reached on the 31st of December, 1994. As far as I remember, our responsibility was to produce daily reports to show whether agreements were complied with and to what extent exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, the first sentence, what does it say there? What is being ordered there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: "Ensure that all provisions in the agreement are fully and consistently adhered to with regard to the Muslim forces and not implement or observe the agreement on the cessation of firing activities in the part of the front where we have a border with the armed forces of the NDH and the HR HB until the territories occupied by the joint forces of the NDH and HR HB are liberated." Therefore, this is clearly in reference to the two parts. The agreement concerning the clashes against the Muslim forces with a total cessation of hostilities being ordered here and the other part of the conflict in the Krajina regarding clashes with the regular units of the Croatian army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any agreements signed with those parties on possible cease-fires or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: No, because representatives of the Croatian army - mind you, I'm not talking about the HVO here, I'm talking about the Army of the Republic of Croatia - being actively involved in the fighting in the Krajina area and those municipalities over there. They were no parties to any of the agreements that were actually signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 4, what is being forbidden in the strictest of terms there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: "I strictly forbid opening fire and carrying out offensive operations in the front line towards the Muslims ..." I think it's probably an error here in spelling, "which would violate the agreement reached. Respond to their possible fire if absolutely necessary and if the lives of combatants and civilians are at peril or if there is a danger of destruction or seizure of combat equipment." So this is a very clear-cut order. Strict compliance with this agreement is demanded here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In relation to this document can you tell us more about what the committees these are that are mentioned here and were you a member of any of these?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the Serbian text pulled up a little and it's also the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To make sure this agreement was actually acted upon and to make sure it wasn't dead in the water since it was signed at the highest level. In each of the corps committees were set up whose duty it was to monitor the implementation of these agreements and implementation consistency as well. I myself was a member of this committee for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You talked about the Croatian army being involved in the occupation of the western municipalities. Were UNPROFOR aware of this and was there anything they did about that in terms of preventing a foreign army from occupying Bosnian territory, or rather, Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: This was a fact that was definitely well-known to everyone there. I don't know personally whether anything at all was done to prevent this from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this be admitted, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2786, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, in your official capacity, did you ever come across issues related to supplies, water and electricity, for Sarajevo specifically regarding both sides? Did you take part in negotiations regarding that, so restoring the supply of electricity and water to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite frequently as a matter of fact. During the first stage after the outbreak of war, the electricity and water facilities were destroyed. As soon as conditions were in place to have those repaired and rebuilt, we demanded that steps be taken in that direction. Each time a formal request was submitted, this would normally go through the liaison officer, the simple reason being most of the damage that had occurred was in the area that was between the confrontation lines. It was necessary, therefore, to use the existing chain of command to order a cease-fire so that the workers could actually go out and get the work done, get the necessary repairs done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did UNPROFOR understand which of the parties was actually sabotaging the repair works?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the UNPROFOR engineers, so the people who were actually in charge, understood very clearly that the lack of co-operation was to be blamed on the Muslim side for the most part. We were talking about infrastructure facilities here and that was a vital issue also from a media perspective when trying to construe an image of yourself as a victim.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D6523 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what this telegram is about, what it means and what it talks about.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: This is a report on a meeting with General Tolimir at Sokolac. I attended this meeting. And aside from other issues, we discussed the possibility of getting on with infrastructure renewal and repair work in and around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to paragraph 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what Tolimir discusses here.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Tolimir says that it's absurd to talk about restoring utilities before a cease-fire is accomplished because whatever is repaired on one day on the next day would be destroyed again because the electric lines were -- ran along the confrontation line right next to it, so it was impossible to work on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the infrastructure system or the infrastructure facilities, were they connected and were there shortages also on the Serbian side, in the Serbian part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, Sarajevo was a large whole before the war, it was one whole, so that the system of infrastructure automatic -- was one whole and automatically a breakdown in one would automatically cause a breakdown in the entire system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago you said that the Muslim party had some political benefits or reaped some political advantage from the fact of this breakdown in supply of water and electricity and what was the Serb response to this in the international media?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately the media were not really very much interested in trying to establish the situation, what the situation was like in the Serbian side and to report that there were similar problems on the Serb side. For instance, when I moved to Banja Luka I learned that at the time when the media reported on the major difficulties in Sarajevo because the power lines were down and there was no electricity, at that same time Banja Luka had been into a full year almost without any electric power and there were no reports on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant-Colonel, did you have any impression on the number of flights and the number of convoys that arrived at the airport in Sarajevo on a daily basis without any difficulties?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, we had a very clear picture of the number of flights and convoys arriving. Even if we were not reported on each and every flight, we did -- we were informed of the convoys. But we also had observers who would count the flights arriving at or landing at the Sarajevo airport. So we had that information as well. Now, as for the convoys that moved in Sarajevo but that did not -- that had not come from the crossing the territory of Republika Srpska, we had no information on them for obvious reasons and we were not responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall how many humanitarian flights and landings at the Sarajevo airport there were on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to give you a figure, but I believe that generally speaking we could say that there were anywhere between five and ten flights a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2787, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I thank you for your understanding and for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Indjic, although some part of your evidence was led live but most of the evidence in chief has been admitted into writing. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, but given the circumstances your cross-examination will be deferred till probably Thursday. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I apologise for your inconvenience, but can I advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I wonder whether the Prosecution might be ready to start their cross tomorrow because I'm a bit concerned about the witness because he's having some difficulties because of his long stay here. If that's not possible, let's leave it as it is, but if at all possible for the Prosecution perhaps it would be more convenient for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just in fairness to Ms. Edgerton, we've gone back and forth on this a couple of times. I'm not precluding that once she has a chance to consider it, but I think that is a question, under the circumstances, that's better left to some reflection and we can get back to the Defence accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. So my understanding is that Mr. Indjic will start his cross-examination on Thursday in any event at least?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, absent any arrangements earlier than that, that's what we would -- at the latest we would ask that he be allowed to testify 9.00 a.m. on Thursday so we're sure to complete his testimony this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we hear from you on that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, not so far but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Tieger said he would come back to me after having consulted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah -- no, you didn't yet and I -- given the pace at which everything has been moving, I didn't ask Ms. Edgerton to address that just yet. So that's -- that same suggestion is pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, I'm sure there won't be a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I wanted to hear. Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. You may be excused, Mr. Indjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're waiting for the next witness I just wanted to add that basically our position on these changes is that when we are the cause of the problem we are ready to accommodate the Prosecutor with -- and they constantly accommodated us during their case in the same way. So whatever time Ms. Edgerton needs within the reasonable limitations we're prepared to accommodate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We were actually -- we were actually just discussing the temperature in the courtroom, Your Honour. It's extremely warm in here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They thought that Judge Lattanzi would be in today.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I appreciate the unique status of this witness, but in conformity with our previous practice, given some aspects -- given the scope of the -- what I would imagine is the intended testimony, I would -- and I also appreciate the presence of the witness's counsel, but it would appear in keeping with our previous practice that an advisement would be -- would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber prefers to be informed of that notice in advance in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And we object to that with respect to this witness because his evidence cannot be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please put it up a bit. I can't hear very well. I have difficulty hearing. [In English] Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can discuss it in the presence of the witness. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. My point is that under Rule 90(H) those protections wouldn't apply to this witness because he has already been convicted of the crimes about which he will be speaking, and therefore to tell him that these can be used to incriminate him is not really accurate because he couldn't be prosecuted again for those same events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is rather advising of his rights than a warning and if there are matters not covered by the previous trial, the Rule has room to be applied even theoretically. But before we proceed further, for the record I would like the counsel for the witness to introduce himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, and to everyone in the courtroom. My name is Stephane Bourgon and I am here to assist and represent the witness, General Dragomir Milosevic. Present with me here in the courtroom this afternoon, as requested yesterday, my interpreter, in case I have to deal with the witness during the hearing, Mr. Milan Kunjevic. And I also have a legal assistant who will be taking notes for me, Mr. Hugo Lagace. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Milosevic, before you start giving evidence I would like to draw your attention to a particular Rule here at the Tribunal. Maybe you are already aware of this, but under this Rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the accused, the Prosecution, or even the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in such a case the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony.
