Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. Everything is all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please feel free to remind me when the pause that I make after your answer is too brief to ensure that every word spoken here will make it into the transcript. Now, if you look at the screen you can see that once my question is complete, there will be a letter A appearing below it. Now, could you please tell us your first and last name and your father's name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Dragomir Milosevic. My father's name is Milorad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were you born and when?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Ub municipality -- my apology, I started earlier. So I was born in Ub municipality in the village of Murgas, the Republic of Serbia, on the 4th of February, 1942.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us something about your background and your education? Could you tell us what schools and where you attended and completed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I began my schooling in elementary school in the place where I was born, of course. I'm talking about the elementary education, elementary school. Then I attended the high school or the secondary school, military secondary school, in Sarajevo. This was in 1958 to be more precise. After completing the secondary military school for a while, or rather, for two years I served in Banja Luka as a non-commissioned officer. At -- in those days, certain cadres could be sent further on to the military academy for further education. I was offered and given this possibility because I met all the conditions. I accepted and I signed up or enrolled at the military academy in Belgrade, which lasted four years. Out of those four years, one, the final year, the senior year, was in Sarajevo. And this was by way of completing a specialised course. Once I graduated from the military academy, I was assigned to the garrison in Ljubljana. Would this be sufficient or would you like me to tell you something about my various appointments?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, could you please tell us what your various appointments were and where you served.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When I arrived in Ljubljana, I was a platoon commander for a while. And soon thereafter I became a company commander. I stayed at the Ljubljana garrison in Sentilj two years, after which I was selected or perhaps there was a decision made - I don't know exactly what the wording was - but I was reassigned to the school for reserve officers in Bileca. I assumed that it was observed that I had certain talents to work with -- to work training personnel. I spent two years in Bileca, where I was platoon commander and company commander. And I spent an entire period of five years there. Following this, I moved to Sarajevo, where I became a member of a military police battalion that was established as a unit that was to serve the needs of the 7th Army, the then-Yugoslav People's Army. I remained there, or rather, I was first appointed deputy commander of the military police battalion and subsequently, after a number -- some time, I can't recall exactly how much time, I became the military police battalion commander. In other words, this was a battalion of the 7th Army. After that, someone decided that I was now at a point where I had met all these other conditions. And then I was transferred to Lukavica near Sarajevo to act as the Chief of Staff in the 49th Regiment. Let me just confirm about all these other things too. In the meantime I had undergone additional training at Belgrade for a two-year duration. It's called the higher military academy. So it was a military political school. After serving with the 49th Motorised Regiment at Lukavica, I was transferred to the Han Pijesak garrison to serve there as commander of the 216th Mountain Brigade. I believe this was back in 1988, and then on from that point in time until the war in Sarajevo broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did I understand you correctly, you arrived in Sarajevo when you were 16. And apart from the time you spent in Ljubljana and apart from your training in Belgrade, all your posts were in Bosnia and Herzegovina, such as Banja Luka and Han Pijesak. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is entirely right. All the other posts were in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I spent more time in Bosnia and Herzegovina than anywhere else as a matter of fact, apart from the time that I have spent in The Hague by now of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, on the 20th of May, 1992, the JNA was withdrawing from Bosnia and Herzegovina. What was the choice that you faced at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's not really that I had much of a choice. It was about me taking a decision, but I know what you mean. People serving in the JNA at the time had certain rights and people who were from one of the republics were free to go back to their own home republic and continue their service there. But members from Bosnia and Herzegovina obviously were also allowed to stay in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I'm not entirely clear about this. How should I interpret the fact that I stayed in Bosnia and Herzegovina? But I don't think that really is the deal-breaker here. I don't think it's that important for me to explain really. It's just a decision that I took. I was constantly hoping that at some point I would be transferred to Belgrade, though. If I may just add one thing, since the question you asked was quite specific. I was a brigade commander. The 216th Brigade stationed at Han Pijesak was subject to a decision taken by the superior command and there was to be mobilisation there back in 1991. So that was a whole year before the clashes in Sarajevo ever broke out, Sarajevo and the rest of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well. So the brigade was mobilised. So it was in a state of semi-combat readiness, so to say, pursuant to this order from our superior command, needless to say. So during this time I was working with these people, I was training them, I was looking after them, and they were working with me as well. So having said and considered all of that, it would have been perhaps immoral of me to have gone through all of this with these men and as soon as certain things happened for me to simply be gone, to up sticks and leave the area, because these people placed an enormous amount of trust in me, and I did not want to let them down and make it seem as though I was leaving them in the lurch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. We'll get back to some questions regarding the war itself. Were you commended for your work? Did you receive any medals or awards?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can't give you the whole list, to be perfectly frank. I don't think I'd be able to think back and remember each and every one, you know, like the specific type of medal that I was awarded or, indeed, the names of these medals and commendations. But I got everything that was due me given my rank and my professional stature at each stage of my career. My professional assessments were always exceptionally favourable. It was always outstanding or even particularly outstanding at one point in time. Sometimes perhaps it would have been wiser to not receive this rating of particularly outstanding because my life might have taken a different course, but I'm just telling you what exactly happened and we can't change the facts. So that of all these medals and commendations being awarded also during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, during the armed conflict there, I remember two specific decorations, the Karadjordje Star, which is a first-grade or second-grade decoration, and also the Milos Obilic medal. I remember those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One is for exercising command, for setting an example; and the other is for courage. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, command and courage, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I see you have some documents in front of you or what is that, a note pad? Let's see what that is and whether perhaps you'd be allowed to use it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is just a blank note pad. There is nothing in it. But yes, I do have some documents here in a folder which I've put together for myself, just in case I get into a situation where I need to interpret some things, perhaps make assertions or perhaps demonstrate certain things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you put these together yourself or was there someone who gave you a hand with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I put them together myself, needless to say, on my own. You need to keep in mind the fact that I am in prison and the people there were not able to help me with this because they know nothing about this, so I was left to my own devices. I came up with a plan and I put together everything that I believed might come in handy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you perhaps jog your memory with respect to the specific documents that you used when you were producing these notes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us try and clarify this. There were all these documents that were used at my trial. I have a memory of all these documents, obviously, but when I was preparing for possibly giving evidence I did not exactly have any of these documents physically available to me. So I wasn't using physical documents. I was trying to think back and remember and not really tie myself down to a specific detail but to think more in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, as you know, written evidence under 92 ter is also admitted by this Tribunal. Did you perhaps produce a written statement specifically for your evidence here in this trial and what about that document right in front of you, is that perhaps the statement that you put together?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me be specific about this. I'm not saying that I'm familiar with all these Rules, 96 bis I think you mentioned or something like that, but it doesn't really matter. I'm in a position to confirm that generally I understand the Rules. But I wanted to come up with some sort of a framework for myself and it didn't matter to me very much whether it was pursuant to this rule or that. I tried to put together a number of things that I could use as reminders just to make sure I remained within the right context. So as far as I understand, you're asking me if this is a statement, a written statement. No, it's just all these things that I was going through while preparing for my own private needs, my notes that would help me find my feet in any situation that I might encounter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General, did anyone specifically ask you to prepare these?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, no one asked me to do this. No one proposed that I do this. No one imposed this on me. No one cautioned me about this. No one even advised me to do it, so the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, may General Milosevic please be allowed to use his notes during his evidence before this Trial Chamber as he goes about answering my questions? As far as I understand, the notes were disclosed to the OTP last Sunday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, do you have any observation to make?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Based on Dr. Karadzic's answer, we did receive a copy of these and a draft translation on the 21st, so no, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber sees no problem with it either as long as you can -- you consult with your handwritten notes under the control of the Chamber. There should be no problem. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I asked my advisors and assistants to get in touch with you and to ask you whether you were prepared to appear as a Defence witness in this trial. They got back to me in no time at all to inform me that you willingly accepted this request. Can you tell me why?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is true that I welcomed the request. No additional information was required for me to agreed to appear in this trial as a Defence witness. As far as my decision to testify here in this trial, well I have quite a number of reasons. As I said, my reasons are numerous and I will only mention here the two principal reasons. I thought about it, I made my assessment, and I arrived at some conclusions. My own trial and the circumstances under which a conviction was imposed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters didn't understand your last sentence. Could you start repeat from your own trial and the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My trial happened and then it was completed. My experience and my conclusion is that certain conclusions were reached at that trial and the conviction was reached that does not conform with what was supposed to be demonstrated and proven beyond reasonable doubt during that trial. Essentially what was missing all together was a faithful depiction of the armed conflict: Who were the clashing parties, what was the progress of the clashes, what were the respective forces involved, and who was involved in the fighting. So a context was concocted, if I can put it that way, suggesting that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps used all of its fire-power to target the civilian population and the civilian infrastructure. I don't think we ever reached a point in that trial where everything that was going on became clear and obvious for all. Because everything that was happening there at the time was against the background of two armed forces clashing. On the one hand the 1st Corps of the BH army and the remaining forces, the police forces and the rest; and on the other the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. These are the two clashing elements or two clashing forces that were engaged in war, in fighting. The issue of civilians belongs to a different context, not that one. So that is what I need in order to be able to be here and offer evidence in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you have a chance to contribute to the creation of a more faithful depiction of historical events during your own trial?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is my problem, isn't it? And that is what I'm trying to confirm. My defence - and I'm not necessarily saying that they did not desire to do so or perhaps they weren't able to achieve that, but my Defence failed to produce evidence really showing and demonstrated what happened there at the time. The option they decided to take was to have an opportunity to challenge those incidents at trial without producing key evidence, key evidence showing who was clashing with whom, to what extent, what exactly was the fierceness of the armed combat involved, what were the intentions of the parties involved, who was sending their forces in which direction, and what were the objectives that they were trying to achieve. We did not arrive at a complete description of what actually happened. So sometimes there was manipulation. Sometimes some things were being staged and offensives were being launched. And it's also about the seriousness of this conflict. Because what actually happened from our perspective was not two forces clashing on equal footing. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had to cover a very extensive area and there was an element of overstretch. We were more than fully stretched, which led to a certain -- to a certain evolution, and that evolution led to different conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if my understanding is correct. Is this something that you understood during the actual trial or was it only after the trial that you arrived at these conclusions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I did not know at the beginning what was going on there. It was during the actual clashes that I understood and I'm sure the enemy understood as well what they were doing and what their intentions were as well as who they were dealing with and the ratio in terms of power between the respective forces involved in the fighting, not to mention the trial itself. I made an enormous effort to make sure my Defence and my Defence team understood what they were meant to do. They were supposed to develop certain method of using documents, taking into account everything that happened in order to portray the situation as it was, as a faithful reflection of our goals, our intentions, our desires, and the decisions that we took at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to appear as a witness in your own trial; and if not, why?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to get something done if you don't enjoy support, if you have no support coming from anywhere and no one to help you -- or rather, allow me to clarify. It's not just about whether I was actually willing to testify or not. What I wanted to do was to tell the Prosecution about this whole situation and tell them what it was like, but they were trying to throw me off track, as it were. Okay. So I would like to own up to something and then, you know, it's totally different. So I didn't want this process to involve any confessions or anything like that, any steps like that being taken, but I wanted to have someone who would hear me out so that I could tell them what actually happened. And then they could take that information and press on in any direction they liked regarding me or, indeed, anything else, no matter whether they would actually believe me or not. So my lawyer tried to talk me out of that. He discouraged me by telling me that this would be no use at all and that it would be an error for me to take that course of action. I didn't understand at the time what exactly that meant, to appear as a witness in your own trial. How far would anyone be willing to trust my words, trust my evidence? Perhaps I would have been construed as trying to lead biased evidence in my favour, but that was all I was trying to achieve. Nothing else mattered. It wasn't like I was trying to take a distance from anything that I did at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Last question today. General, sir, let's leave theory aside and probably no good lawyer would advise you to trust the Prosecutor, but could it perhaps have been the case that there were documents for you to use that perhaps you might have used during your own evidence in your own trial and yet those documents were never actually produced during the trial?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Documents are something special, something important, something big. My Defence team told me at one point that they had collected a total of 5.000 documents from the defence ministry in Sarajevo. I was overjoyed. 5.000 documents. And now it was time for me to study these documents, to go through them, and to make certain suggestions in line with that to my Defence team, but I didn't get that chance. So it was all about the plan hatched up by the person in charge of my Defence. He wanted to take the shortest route in order to keep us from wasting time because all this needs translating and so on and so forth. So he came up with a selection of documents and then I went through those documents and then told him what I thought he should do. But when I continued to make suggestions, they simply paid no heed. He had his own plan. He wasn't interested in my plan, in my ideas. Every time I would propose that he seek out someone, an expert or a person to talk to, I always got the same reply. Invariably, he would tell me that those were people who came to him for advice because he was the cleverest guy around and it wasn't his job to go around asking other people for advice. So I didn't have all these documents available to me apart from the ones that he was actually tendering, but I'd normally first set eyes on those in the courtroom and not before. So how could I use any of those as evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General, sir. I believe this is all the time that we've got for today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we pressing on until 3.00, Your Excellency, or is it quarter to 3.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for today. Mr. Milosevic, I'd like to advise you once you started giving evidence you're not supposed to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. The hearing ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of course that excludes your counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I intend to visit the witness at the Detention Unit. However, it's already been explained to the witness that this is for his well being and not to discuss contents of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 23rd day of January, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.52 p.m.,
